html:
The Lunda Empire was a confederation of states in the southern savanna of Central Africa, in what are now the south-west of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, north-east Angola and north-west Zambia. The map shows it from 1530 to 1900.

Lunda tradition says a Luba hunter prince, Chibinda Ilunga, married the Lunda queen Lueji, and that their line founded the kingship. Most of this lies in legend, but the Lunda clearly borrowed ideas of sacred kingship from the Luba to the north-east. The ruler took the title Mwata Yamvo.

The empire's strength was a flexible system. Conquered chiefs kept their posts and paid tribute, and Lunda princes were sent out to found new kingdoms, such as Kazembe on the Luapula River to the east. This let Lunda power spread far without a large army.

Lunda sat in the middle of the continent, trading with both coasts:

  • west to the Portuguese at Luanda and Benguela, selling captives into the Atlantic slave trade in return for cloth and guns;
  • east, through Kazembe, toward the Swahili coast.

New crops from the Americas, especially cassava, helped feed its capital. In the 1880s the Chokwe, former subjects enriched by the ivory and rubber trade, overran the heartland. The lands were then divided between the Congo Free State, Portuguese Angola and British territory.
